rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Electrolysis is redox driven backwards: a battery forces electrons into the **cathode (negative)**, where cations are reduced, and pulls them from the **anode (positive)**, where anions — or the anode itself — are oxidised; same AN OX/RED CAT chemistry as a galvanic cell, opposite polarity.…

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Anions do not always reach the anode's oxidation:** SO₄²⁻, NO₃⁻ and F⁻ resist discharge — water's OH⁻ is oxidised instead, so oxygen, not the anion's element, appears.  ·  **Concentration bends the rules:** in concentrated brine Cl⁻ out-competes OH⁻ at the anode even though OH⁻ is nominally easier to discharge — the textbook order assumes comparable concentrations.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: "Electrolysis is the process of chemical decomposition of an electrolyte by the passage of electricity: reduction occurs at the cathode and oxidation at the anode."

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***Electrorefining copper*** — an impure anode dissolves, 99.99% copper plates the cathode, silver and gold collect as "anode mud" worth more than the copper itself.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Forcing Reactions Backwards with Electricity Spontaneous redox runs a galvanic cell; electricity can also **drive non-spontaneous redox** — that is electrolysis. Pass a current through molten NaCl and sodium metal appears at one electrode, chlorine gas at the other; pass it through CuSO₄ solution and copper plates out.…  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 The electrolytic cell - **Electrolysis:** chemical decomposition by passage of direct current through an electrolyte (molten or aqueous). - **Cathode:** the **negative** electrode in electrolysis — **reduction** happens here (cations migrate to it, gain electrons). - **Anode:** the **positive** electrode — **oxidation** happens here (anions migrate, lose electrons).…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Polarity: "electrolysis cathode = minus". Discharge ladder: "Cu H Pb Fe Zn Na K" at the cathode; "OH I Br Cl SO4 F" at the anode. Classic products table: molten NaCl → Na/Cl₂; CuSO₄/Pt → Cu/O₂; CuSO₄/Cu → Cu/Cu²⁺; H₂SO₄ → 2:1.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Electrolysis: current decomposes molten/aqueous electrolyte; electrical → chemical. Cathode − (reduction, cations); anode + (oxidation, anions); AN OX/RED CAT with polarity opposite to galvanic. Preferential discharge: cathode order Cu²⁺ > H⁺ > Pb²⁺ > Fe²⁺ > Zn²⁺ > Na⁺ > K⁺; anode OH⁻ > I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > SO₄²⁻/F⁻.…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Aluminium exists in aircraft only because electrolysis (Hall–Héroult, molten Al₂O₃ in cryolite) can force the reverse of thermite's favourite reaction — electricity beating the series.

rows.text: **NEB-style (2m): State the preferential discharge order of cations at the cathode and explain one practical consequence.** — The ease of discharge at the cathode follows the electrochemical series from bottom (most easily reduced) upward: **Cu²⁺ > H⁺ > Pb²⁺ > Fe²⁺ > Zn²⁺ > Na⁺ > Ca²⁺ > K⁺** — ions…

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ## 6. Common Confusions **Cathode is negative — but only in electrolysis:** in a galvanic cell the cathode is positive. The process (reduction at cathode) never changes; the sign does. Always state the cell type.  ·  **Na⁺ rarely discharges from water:** in aqueous NaCl the hydrogen comes from water/H⁺, not sodium — molten salt is required to win sodium metal.  ·  **Anode is where oxidation happens even if the anode itself is the victim:** a copper anode oxidises *into solution* — still oxidation, still the anode.
